items.title: Power BI Course
items.text: Learn Microsoft Power BI from first steps to advanced reporting, DAX (Data Analysis Expressions), and publishing. This site hosts the complete course material, organized to take you from installation to interactive, production-ready reports.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
This course covers:

  • Installation and setup of Power BI Desktop and Service
  • Data loading, shaping, and modeling with relationships and DAX
  • Core visuals, filters, slicers, and visual calculations
  • Interactive dashboards, publishing, and app workspaces
  • Integrations with Excel and PowerPoint
  • Hands-on activities with provided datasets and solutions

items.title: 1. Getting Started with Power BI
items.text:
Set up your environment and learn the basics.

  • Introduction to Power BI and course objectives
  • Download the training data files
  • Sign up for the Power BI Service
  • Load data into the Power BI Service
  • Practical activity: initial setup

items.title: 2. Power BI Desktop Overview
items.text:
Understand the desktop interface and configuration.

  • Options and settings
  • Interface layout and main panes

items.title: 3. Working with Tables
items.text:
Create, format, and analyze data with tables.

  • Table creation and formatting
  • Cross-filtering and aggregation
  • Practical activities and solutions

items.title: 4. Visualizations -- Matrix and Cards
items.text:
Build summary views for KPIs and dimensional analysis.

  • Matrix visuals and configuration
  • Card visuals for single-value metrics
  • Practical exercises and solutions

items.title: 5. Dates and Visual Calculations
items.text:
Work effectively with dates and built-in visual calculations.

  • Date management and formatting
  • Visual-level calculations and use cases
  • Practical setup and scenarios

items.title: 6. Filters and Slicers
items.text:
Control scope and interactivity for analysis.

  • Text, numeric, and date slicers
  • Visual-, page-, and report-level filters
  • Practical activities with solutions

items.title: 7. Graph Visualizations
items.text:
Create charts for comparison, composition, and trends.

  • Clustered, stacked, and 100 percent charts
  • Options, trend analysis, and forecasting
  • Reference lines and additional chart types
  • Practical challenges and solutions

items.title: 8. Interactive Dashboards and Reports
items.text:
Design, publish, and share interactive experiences.

  • Building interactive dashboards and reports
  • Publishing to the Power BI Service
  • Pinning visuals to dashboards
  • Mobile reports, Q&A visuals, app workspaces, and themes
  • Using custom visuals

items.title: 9. Data Modeling -- Columns and Measures
items.text:
Model data with DAX for robust analytics.

  • Calculated columns and measures
  • Date functions and master date tables
  • The CALCULATE function and DAX query view
  • Hands-on activities with solutions

items.title: 10. Relationships and Data Transformation
items.text:
Connect and shape data for reliable models.

  • Creating and managing relationships
  • Relationship calculations
  • Query Editor for data transformation
  • Summary tables

items.title: 11. Integration with Other Tools
items.text:
Extend analysis and presentation.

  • Power BI with Excel
  • Power BI with PowerPoint

items.title: Purpose and Scope
items.text:
This course serves as a structured, comprehensive introduction to Microsoft Power BI, covering both Power BI Desktop and the Power BI Service. It is designed for business analysts, data professionals, and technical users aiming to develop skills in interactive reporting, data modeling, and dashboard publishing using Microsoft’s self-service BI platform.

You will learn to transform raw datasets into dynamic, shareable insights using Power BI’s end-to-end capabilities—ranging from data transformation and modeling, to advanced visualization and report deployment.

items.title: Tutorials Components
items.text: The tutorial is divided into several sequential modules that provide both theoretical understanding and practical, hands-on skills across the Power BI stack:

items.title: Overview of Power BI Ecosystem
items.text:
• Power BI Desktop: A Windows application for data import, modeling, and report design
  • Power BI Service: A cloud-based platform for report sharing, collaboration, and governance

  • Overview includes:

  • Interface orientation

  • Key functional differences
  • Integration between Desktop and Service

items.title: Core Visualizations and Formatting
items.text:
You will work with various data visual elements to create rich, interactive reports:

Visualization Type Features Covered Tables Data listings, conditional formatting Matrix Hierarchical row/column structure with measures Cards Single-value KPIs, formatting for performance metrics Column/Bar Charts Comparative graphical representation Line Charts Trend analysis and time series visualizations

Formatting techniques include:

  • Data label configuration
  • Title, border, and background styling
  • Color encoding for business context

items.title: Filters and Interactivity
items.text:
Power BI supports multiple methods of filtering and interactivity:

  • Report-level filters
  • Page-level filters
  • Visual-level filters

  • Slicers:

  • Dynamic user filters via dropdowns, sliders, or checkboxes

  • Cross-filtering:

  • Clickable visuals that impact other visual components

You will learn to build fully interactive reports that dynamically respond to user actions.

items.title: Publishing and Enhancing Reports in the Service
items.text:
After report development, we transition to Power BI Service:

  • Publishing Reports from Desktop
  • Creating Dashboards by pinning visuals

  • Q&A Feature:

  • Natural language querying of datasets

  • App Workspaces:

  • Organize and collaborate on BI content

  • Define access roles (Admin, Member, Viewer)

  • Publishing Apps:

  • Packaged reports and dashboards for end-users

items.title: Data Modeling Fundamentals
items.text:
A critical part of Power BI development lies in semantic modeling. You will:

  • Create Calculated Columns:

  • Row-context based computations stored in the table

  • Create Measures:

  • Aggregation logic applied at runtime to visualizations

  • Define Relationships between tables
  • Understand cardinality and filter propagation
  • Implement Data Normalization Best Practices

items.title: External Integration
items.text:
You will also explore how Power BI integrates with other productivity tools:

  • Excel:

  • Export to Excel

  • Analyze in Excel with OLAP connections

  • PowerPoint:

  • Export report visuals to slides

  • Maintain interactivity via Power BI add-ins

items.title: Power Query Editor
items.text:
The course introduces Power Query, also known as the Query Editor, for data preparation:

  • Data extraction (from files, databases, web, etc.)

  • Data transformation:

  • Column splitting, pivot/unpivot, change types

  • Data cleaning:

  • Remove duplicates, handle nulls

  • Merge and append queries
  • Applied Steps and M Code fundamentals

items.title: Prerequisites and Environment Setup
items.text:
• No programming knowledge required
  • Windows 10+ required for Power BI Desktop
  • Microsoft account (work email) required for Power BI Service
  • Stable internet connection recommended

items.title: Tutorial Philosophy
items.text:
The course emphasizes a layered approach to learning:

  1. Understand the tools (Power BI Desktop + Service)
  2. Learn to visualize
  3. Learn to interact
  4. Learn to model
  5. Learn to share

items.title: Summary of Learning Objectives
items.text: Module Key Deliverable Power BI Desktop Import, model, and visualize data locally Power BI Service Share, publish, and collaborate on reports Visualization Design Use core and advanced visuals for business storytelling Interactive Reporting Enable filtering and exploration through interactivity Semantic Modeling Create DAX-based logic and define table relationships Data Preparation Clean, shape, and combine data in Power Query Report Distribution Use apps, dashboards, and workspace management Integration Export and enhance reports with Excel and PowerPoint

items.title: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report
items.text:
Comprehensive, step-by-step documentation to:

  1. Create a semantic model (dataset) in Power BI Service from an Excel file.
  2. Build a simple report using a table visual.
  3. Save and locate artifacts in a workspace.
  4. Apply operational best practices and troubleshooting.

No assumptions beyond the provided transcription. Where broader context is useful, it is labeled clearly.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Terminology
items.text:
• Semantic model: The data model stored in the Power BI Service. It backs reports and exposes tables, columns, and relationships.
  • Dataset: Common term historically used for the model in the Service. In this document, "semantic model" is preferred.
  • Report: A set of pages and visuals built on top of a semantic model.
  • Workspace: A container in the Service holding semantic models, reports, dashboards, etc. "My Workspace" is your personal area.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• An Excel workbook containing tabular data. The transcription references a training file (single table on one sheet).
  • Ability to use My Workspace or another workspace where you can create content.

If your Excel file is not already formatted as a table in Excel, the Service can still read a sheet, but tables are recommended for cleaner type inference and column detection.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Data Preparation Checklist (Excel)
items.text:
Recommended before upload:

  • One header row with clear column names.
  • No merged cells in the data region.
  • Values typed consistently per column (dates as dates, numbers as numbers, text as text).
  • If possible, format the data as an Excel Table (Insert > Table). Name it meaningfully (e.g., SalesData).
  • Remove totals/subtotals from the data region. Keep the dataset row-level and add aggregations in Power BI.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Workflow Overview
items.text:
1. Open the Power BI Service and go to a workspace.
  2. Create a new semantic model and choose Excel as the source.
  3. Upload the Excel file (OneDrive recommended, local upload supported per transcription).
  4. Authenticate if requested, then select the table or sheet from the workbook.
  5. Create the semantic model and wait for the load to finish.
  6. Build a simple report (table visual) using fields from the model.
  7. Save the report and confirm both the semantic model and the report exist in the workspace.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Detailed Steps
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Access the Service
items.text:
1. Navigate to https://app.powerbi.com and sign in.

  2. Home page options:

  3. New report (quick start), or

  4. Create menu for more options.

The transcription proceeds via a workspace for clarity and control.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Go to a Workspace
items.text:
1. In the left navigation, select "Workspaces".
  2. Choose "My Workspace".
  3. Click "New item".

You will see options including "Semantic model" (data model), reports, and more.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Create a Semantic Model
items.text:
1. Select "Semantic model".

  2. Choose the data source type. Options shown in the transcription:

  3. Excel

  4. CSV
  5. Paste or manual entry
  6. Select "Excel".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Choose Storage and Upload
items.text:
1. The Service offers to connect from online storage (OneDrive recommended in the transcription).
  2. If your file is local, select "Upload file".
  3. Use "Browse" and pick the Excel file (e.g., training_data.xlsx).
  4. Confirm the selection. The Service uploads the file.
  5. Wait for "Upload success".

Note: OneDrive is recommended in the transcription for easier refresh and updates. Local uploads are supported for this lesson.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Authorize if Prompted
items.text:
1. If "Next" is disabled, click "Sign in".
  2. Authorize your account.
  3. Once authorized, the "Next" button is enabled. Click "Next".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Select Workbook Objects
items.text:
1. The Service scans for:

  2. Tables (preferred)

  3. Sheets
  4. Select the table if available. The transcription notes that the table and sheet contained the same data.

  5. Review the preview:

  6. Verify column names.

  7. Confirm data types (dates show as date, numeric as decimal, text as text).
  8. Click "Create".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Load and Validate
items.text:
1. The Service performs:

  2. Preparing

  3. Loading
  4. Finishing

  5. After completion:

  6. Open the model-backed report canvas.

  7. In the right pane, confirm the table (e.g., Data 1) and its fields are visible.
  8. Visualizations and Filters panes are available.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Build a Simple Report (Table)
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Insert a Table Visual
items.text:
1. On the canvas, select the "Table" visual.

  2. With the visual selected:

  3. Click a categorical field (e.g., Manufacturer) to add it to the table.

  4. Drag a numeric field (e.g., Sales) into the visual or into the "Values" well.

Result: Sales are aggregated by Manufacturer. The default aggregation for numeric fields is sum.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Basic Formatting and Interaction (Optional)
items.text:
• Sorting: Use the column header dropdown or sort icon on the visual.
  • Aggregation: If a numeric column aggregates incorrectly, change it in the Values well (e.g., Sum, Average, Count) or set it to "Do not summarize" when appropriate.
  • Resizing: Drag handles on the visual to resize. Expand the canvas region by minimizing the Filters pane for more space.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Save and Locate Artifacts
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Save the Report
items.text:
1. Click the disk icon.
  2. Enter a name (e.g., "My Report").
  3. Click "Save".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Confirm in Workspace
items.text:
1. Return to "My Workspace".

  2. You should now see:

  3. The semantic model (the uploaded and created model from Excel).

  4. The report (the one you saved).
  5. Open the report from the workspace. To edit, click "Edit" in the toolbar.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Operational Guidance
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Storage Choice and Refresh
items.text:
• OneDrive/SharePoint Online: Recommended in the transcription for simpler update cycles. Edits to the workbook can be surfaced with minimal effort.
  • Local upload: Suitable for quick tests or static data. To update, repeat the upload or replace the file as applicable.

For routine updates, keep source files online (OneDrive/SharePoint). This reduces manual steps for data refresh in the Service.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Workspace Organization
items.text:
• Use clear, consistent names:

  • Semantic model: e.g., "TrainingData_SemanticModel"

  • Report: e.g., "TrainingData_Report"
  • Add descriptions in workspace item settings to document source and purpose.
  • Use folders or naming prefixes to distinguish environments (e.g., DEV_, TEST_, PROD_) if working outside "My Workspace".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Data Types and Quality
items.text:
• Verify that dates, numbers, and text appear as expected in the preview.

  • If types are incorrect in the Service preview:

  • Adjust the source Excel types and re-upload, or

  • For complex transformations, prepare data with Power BI Desktop or dataflows before publishing to the Service.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Visual Construction Tips
items.text:
• Start with one visual to validate the model behaves as expected.

  • Use fields with distinct roles:

  • Dimensions (e.g., Manufacturer) for grouping.

  • Measures or numeric columns (e.g., Sales) for aggregation.
  • Add filters or slicers after validating the base table, if needed.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Troubleshooting
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: "Next" Button Disabled
items.text:
• Cause: Not signed in for authorization.
  • Action: Click "Sign in", authorize, retry.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: No Tables Found
items.text:
• Cause: The workbook may not contain a defined table object; only a sheet is present.
  • Action: Select the sheet. If the sheet preview looks incorrect, format the range as a table in Excel and re-upload.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Data Types Misdetected
items.text:
• Cause: Mixed or ambiguous values in a column.
  • Action: Clean values in Excel, ensure consistent typing, then re-upload.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Upload Dialog Off-Screen
items.text:
• Cause: Screen capture or window sizing issue (noted in the transcription).
  • Action: Use the system file picker, choose the file, confirm "Open".
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Fields Not Aggregating As Expected
items.text:
• Cause: Default summarization may not match intent.
  • Action: In the Values well, set aggregation explicitly (Sum, Average, Count, Do not summarize).
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Report Not Visible After Save
items.text:
• Cause: Saved to another workspace or save failed.
  • Action: Verify the current workspace, refresh the workspace list, confirm item names.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Best Practices
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Before Upload
items.text:
• Clean, typed columns in Excel.
  • Use an Excel Table for the data region.
  • Avoid calculated totals in the raw table.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: During Model Creation
items.text:
• Prefer "Table" over "Sheet" when both exist.
  • Verify previewed data types.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: After Model Creation
items.text:
• Validate a simple table visual end-to-end.
  • Name and save artifacts clearly.
  • Keep source files in online storage for easier updates.

For advanced modeling, consider preparing the model in Power BI Desktop or using dataflows, then publishing to the Service.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Quick Reference
items.text:
• Create model: Workspace > New item > Semantic model > Excel.
  • Upload: Upload file > Browse > Select workbook > Upload success.
  • Authorize: Sign in if prompted > Next enabled.
  • Select objects: Choose Table (preferred) or Sheet > Preview > Create.
  • Build: Add Table visual > Add categorical field(s) + numeric field(s).
  • Save: Disk icon > Name report > Save.
  • Locate: Workspace shows both semantic model and report.
path: Loading Excel Data and Building a Report

items.title: Notes and Limits
items.text:
• This document follows the exact flow in the transcription: semantic model creation from an Excel file in the Power BI Service, then a single table visual, and save.
  • Capacity limits, licensing nuances, and refresh scheduling specifics are not included here. I do not have access to that information.

items.title: Introduction
items.text: Power BI is a cloud-based business intelligence platform by Microsoft that supports real-time analytics, reporting, and data visualization. This documentation focuses on Power BI Service, the SaaS component accessed via a web browser, and how users can effectively sign up, navigate, create, and manage content in a scalable, enterprise-compliant manner.

items.title: Signing Up for Power BI Service
Website Access
items.text:
• Navigate to: https://powerbi.microsoft.com

  • Entry points available:

  • "Sign In" (top-right, mid-screen, and footer)

  • "Try Free" for new registrations

items.title: Account Prerequisites
items.text: Requirement Detail Email Type Must use a work or organizational email (e.g., name@company.com) Personal Emails Domains such as Gmail, Yahoo, or Outlook.com are not supported Tenant Access Power BI requires an Azure Active Directory (AAD) tenant association

items.title: Registration Flow
items.text:
1. Click “Try Free”
  2. Provide a valid organizational email
  3. Complete Microsoft account setup (if needed)
  4. Verify email address
  5. Gain access to Power BI Service as a Free or Pro trial user

items.title: Understanding the Power BI Service UI
Primary Sections
items.text: Section Description Home Personalized content overview: recent, recommended reports, usage trends Favorites Quick access to starred reports and dashboards Create Interface to initiate new report building from datasets or files Browse File system-like navigation across user content, shared content, and apps Workspaces Core collaboration units for storing and managing reports/datasets Apps Packaged BI content published to targeted user groups Metrics KPI and scorecard building area Data Hub Listing of semantic models (datasets) available for reporting Learning Access to tutorials, Microsoft Learn, and training materials Admin/Monitoring For Power BI Admins to track activity, usage, and permissions

items.title: Home Screen Overview
items.text:
• Displays “Recommended” content based on usage frequency
  • Lists “Recent Reports” across workspaces
  • Provides quick-access actions (e.g., add to Favorites, open, share)

items.title: Favorites Management
items.text:
• Mark any report, dashboard, or dataset as a favorite via the star icon
  • Favorites appear in the dedicated “Favorites” section in the navigation pane
  • Toggling the star removes it from favorites

items.title: Browse View
items.text:
• Filters:

  • Recent

  • Favorites
  • Shared with Me
  • Owned by Me

  • Allows:

  • Sorting by type (reports, datasets, dashboards)

  • Searching across titles and metadata

items.title: Creating Content in the Power BI Service
Report Creation from Existing Datasets
items.text:
Steps:

  1. Click Create > Pick a published semantic model
  2. Select an available dataset (published to your workspace or shared)
  3. Enter the web-based report editor
  4. Drag fields into the canvas, configure visuals

items.title: Uploading and Connecting Data
items.text:
Supported methods (covered later in detail):

  • Upload .pbix files from Power BI Desktop
  • Import Excel files
  • Connect to cloud services (SharePoint, Azure SQL, Salesforce)
  • Use Dataflows for ETL within the service

items.title: Definition
items.text:
A workspace is a logical container used for:

  • Group collaboration
  • Content separation by department/function
  • Role-based access control (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer)

items.title: My Workspace
items.text:
• Private to each user
  • Available on both free and paid licenses

  • Intended for:

  • Personal development

  • Local testing

  • Limitations:

  • No sharing unless on a Pro license

  • No access delegation

items.title: Creating a Workspace
items.text:
1. Go to Workspaces > Create a workspace

  2. Define:

  3. Name

  4. Description
  5. Image (optional)
  6. License type (Pro / Premium per user / Premium capacity)
  7. Add users and assign roles

items.title: Use Cases
items.text: Workspace Type Use Case Example Sales Workspace CRM dashboards, lead tracking reports Finance Workspace Budget reports, variance analysis dashboards Project Workspace Sprint tracking, timeline burndown visualizations

• Created in Power BI Desktop

  • Published to:

items.title: Supported Model Features

• Relationships
  • Measures (DAX)

items.text:
• Create visual summaries of key indicators
  • Combine values, goals, and status indicators
  • Ideal for executive dashboards and KPI tracking

items.title: Monitoring (Admin Portal)
items.text:
• For capacity and usage monitoring
  • Audit logs, dataset refresh monitoring
  • Role-based access: Admin only

items.title: Learning Hub
items.text:
• Direct link to Microsoft training
  • Includes interactive modules, certification guides

items.title: Content Organization

• Use dedicated workspaces per department or function

items.title: Data Model Governance

• Encourage reuse of semantic models
  • Centralize dataset ownership for consistency

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Power BI Desktop is the primary authoring tool for creating Power BI reports and dashboards. It runs exclusively on Windows and provides all the capabilities to connect to data sources, transform data, and build interactive visualizations.

This chapter explains how to install Power BI Desktop, perform initial setup, and ensure key features are enabled for an optimal experience.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Installation Requirements
items.text:
• Operating System: Windows (Power BI Desktop is not natively available for macOS or Linux).
  • Internet Connection: Required for downloading updates and connecting to online data sources.
  • Administrator Access: May be needed to install the application on your computer.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Installing Power BI Desktop
items.text: You can install Power BI Desktop in one of two ways:
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Option 1 – Microsoft Store (Recommended)
items.text:
1. Open the Microsoft Store on your Windows device.
  2. Search for Power BI Desktop.
  3. Click Install.
  4. Updates are handled automatically by the Store.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Option 2 – Direct Download
items.text:
1. Visit the official Power BI Download Page.
  2. Download the latest .msi installer.
  3. Run the installer and follow the setup wizard.
  4. Check for updates regularly to keep your version current.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Keeping Power BI Desktop Up to Date
items.text:
Microsoft updates Power BI Desktop monthly, adding new features and improvements. To ensure you have the latest capabilities:

  • If installed via the Microsoft Store, updates are automatic.
  • If installed via direct download, manually check for updates on the Power BI website.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Initial Setup
items.text:
After installing Power BI Desktop:

  1. Launch the Application Open Power BI Desktop from the Start menu or desktop shortcut.

  2. Sign In

  3. Use your organizational or Microsoft account for access to publishing and online features.

  4. Configure Options

  5. Go to File > Options and Settings > Options.

  6. Adjust settings such as:

    • Preview Features: Enable experimental features like Visual Calculations or other tools as needed.
    • Regional Settings: Set default locale, date, and number formats.
    • Global Settings: Adjust data load, privacy levels, and performance options.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Key Points to Check
items.text:
• Preview Features: Some new tools (like Visual Calculations) may need to be manually enabled.
  • Updates: Make sure you are on the latest version to access new monthly features.
  • Settings Backup: Consider noting any changes you make to options in case you reinstall Power BI Desktop.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Summary
items.text: Power BI Desktop is a Windows-only application that receives monthly updates from Microsoft. Installation can be done through the Microsoft Store (automatic updates) or direct download. After installation, configure key settings—especially Preview Features—to take advantage of the latest tools. Ensuring you stay updated guarantees access to new features and improvements for creating and managing Power BI reports efficiently.
path: Power BI Desktop – Installation and Initial Setup

items.title: Options and Settings in Power BI Desktop
path: Options and Settings in Power BI Desktop

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Power BI Desktop ships with a wide range of configuration knobs that let you adapt the tool to your workflow, your organization's policies, and experimental features you want to try. All of them live under File › Options and settings — either in the global Options dialog or in Data source settings.

Reference: Enabling Preview Features in Power BI Desktop – Microsoft Learn
path: Options and Settings in Power BI Desktop

items.title: Navigating to Options
items.text:

items.title: Section Overview
items.text:
Tables are the foundation of data exploration in Power BI. Before reaching for sophisticated visuals, a simple table lets you verify that data is correct, aggregations behave as expected, and fields relate properly.

This section walks through every table-related skill you need:

Topic File Creating a table visual 03_creating_tables.md Styles, formatting, and conditional formatting 03_table_styles_formatting.md Practical activity 03_tables_practical_activity.md Activity answers 03_answers_tables_activity.md Cross-filtering behavior 03_cross_filtering_tables.md Changing aggregation methods 03_change_aggregation.md Aggregation practical activity 03_methods_aggregation_activity.md Aggregation challenge answers 03_methods_aggregation_completed.md

items.title: Why Start with Tables?
items.text:
• Data verification — inspect raw values before building charts.
  • Aggregation clarity — see sums, averages, and counts side-by-side.
  • Cross-filter testing — confirm that clicking one visual filters another correctly.
  • Client-friendly output — stakeholders often request exportable tabular data alongside dashboards.

  • Format column headers, cell backgrounds, fonts, and borders.
  • Apply conditional formatting using background color scales, data bars, and icons.
  • Use cross-filtering to make tables interact with other visuals.
  • Change the aggregation method of numeric columns (Sum, Average, Count, Min, Max, etc.).

items.title: Objective
items.text: Apply the table skills covered in this section to build and format a table visual from the training dataset. By the end of this activity you will have a formatted, interactive table that demonstrates aggregation, conditional formatting, and cross-filter interaction.

items.title: Dataset
items.text:
Use the training Excel file loaded into your Power BI Desktop file. It contains columns such as:

  • Product — product name (text)
  • Category — product category (text)
  • Region — sales region (text)
  • Sales — revenue amount (numeric)
  • Units — quantity sold (numeric)
  • OrderDate — transaction date (date)

items.title: Task 1 — Create a Basic Table
items.text:
1. Open a blank report page. Name it "Tables Activity".
  2. Add a Table visual to the canvas.
  3. Add these fields to the Columns well in order:
  4. Product
  5. Category
  6. Region
  7. Sales
  8. Units
  9. Resize the table to fill roughly half the canvas.
  10. Sort the table by Sales descending.

Expected result: A multi-column table showing products, their categories and regions, and aggregated sales and units, sorted from highest to lowest sales.

items.title: Task 2 — Apply a Style Preset
items.text:
1. With the table selected, open the Format visual pane.
  2. Under Style presets, choose Alternating rows.
  3. Confirm the table now shows banded rows.

items.title: Task 3 — Format Column Headers
items.text:
1. Under Format visual › Column headers:
  2. Set background color to dark grey (e.g., #333333).
  3. Set font color to white (#FFFFFF).
  4. Set font size to 12.
  5. Enable Bold.
  6. Confirm the headers are now white text on a dark background.

items.title: Task 4 — Conditional Formatting on Sales
items.text:
1. In the Columns well, click the chevron (∨) next to Sales.
  2. Select Conditional formatting › Background color.
  3. Set Format style to Gradient.
  4. Choose:
  5. Minimum: white (#FFFFFF)
  6. Maximum: green (#107C10)
  7. Click OK.

Expected result: The Sales column now shades from white (lowest) to green (highest), making top performers visually obvious.

items.title: Task 5 — Add a Data Bar to Units
items.text:
1. Click the chevron next to Units in the Columns well.
  2. Select Conditional formatting › Data bars.
  3. Keep default colors (blue positive bar).
  4. Click OK.

items.title: Task 6 — Add a Second Visual and Test Cross-Filtering
items.text:
1. Add a Clustered column chart to the canvas (Category on X-axis, Sales on Y-axis).
  2. Click a bar in the column chart.
  3. Observe the table filtering to show only rows from that category.
  4. Click the same bar again (or press Esc) to clear the filter.

items.title: Checklist
items.text: Task Done Table created with 5 fields ☐ Sorted by Sales descending ☐ Alternating rows style applied ☐ Header formatted (dark/white/bold) ☐ Conditional formatting on Sales ☐ Data bars on Units ☐ Cross-filter tested with column chart ☐

items.title: Tips
items.text:
• If a column shows "Sum of Sales" in the header, you can rename it: click the field in the Columns well, choose Rename for this visual, and type a cleaner name like "Revenue".
  • If totals row aggregation looks wrong for a measure, check the DAX expression — totals evaluate at the grand total filter context, not as a sum of row values.

items.title: Overview
items.text: This page provides the expected outcomes and guidance for each task in the Tables Practical Activity. Use it to verify your work or to understand the correct approach if you encountered difficulties.

items.title: Steps taken
items.text:
1. Added a new report page named "Tables Activity".
  2. Selected the Table visual icon in the Visualizations pane.
  3. Added fields in order: Product → Category → Region → Sales → Units.
  4. Clicked the Sales column header once — the arrow pointed up (ascending). Clicked again — arrow pointed down (descending). Table now shows highest-sales products first.

Key point: Sorting is applied per visual and is saved with the report. When a user opens the report, they will see the table already sorted descending by Sales.

items.title: Task 2 — Apply a Style Preset
items.text:
Format visual › Style presets › Alternating rows

The banded row effect alternates between white and a light grey or the accent color defined in your report theme. This is purely cosmetic — it does not change data or filtering behavior.

items.title: Task 3 — Format Column Headers
items.text:
Settings applied:

Setting Value Background color #333333 (dark grey) Font color #FFFFFF (white) Font size 12 Bold On

Troubleshooting: If the header color is not changing, ensure you are in the Format visual tab (paint roller), not the Build visual tab.

items.title: Task 4 — Conditional Formatting on Sales
items.text:
Full path: Columns well → Sales chevron → Conditional formatting → Background color

Setting Value Format style Gradient Minimum color #FFFFFF (white) Maximum color #107C10 (green) Minimum value (Lowest) Maximum value (Highest)

The gradient uses the minimum and maximum values in the currently visible rows. If you filter the table via a slicer, the gradient re-scales to the filtered range — this is expected behavior.

Alternative: If you wanted a fixed scale (e.g., always 0 = white, 100,000 = green), set explicit number values for Minimum and Maximum instead of leaving them as "Lowest/Highest".

items.title: Task 5 — Add a Data Bar to Units
items.text:
Full path: Columns well → Units chevron → Conditional formatting → Data bars

Data bars scale relative to the column minimum and maximum visible in the table. A product with 0 units sold shows no bar; the product with the most units sold shows a full-width bar.

Tip: Enable Show bar only (under data bar settings) if you want a sparkline-like effect without the number cluttering the cell.

items.title: Task 6 — Cross-Filtering
items.text:
Expected behavior:

  • Clicking a bar in the column chart highlights matching rows in the table and dims the others.
  • The table totals row updates to reflect only the filtered records.
  • Right-clicking a bar and selecting Keep only this applies a persistent filter.

How cross-filtering works: By default, Power BI enables cross-highlighting between visuals on the same page. When you click a data point, the other visuals re-evaluate their data against the implicit filter created by that selection.

Reference: How visuals cross-filter each other in a Power BI report – Microsoft Learn

To change cross-filter behavior between two specific visuals:

  1. Select the visual you want to change interaction from.
  2. Go to Format › Edit interactions.
  3. On other visuals, toggle between Filter (funnel icon), Highlight (bar icon), or None (circle with line).

items.title: Overview
items.text:
When you drag a numeric column into a visual, Power BI applies a default aggregation — usually Sum. But many analytical questions require a different function: an average order value, a distinct count of customers, the maximum temperature recorded, or no aggregation at all for ID columns. Understanding how to change and control aggregation is fundamental to building accurate reports.

Reference: Aggregates in Power BI service – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Default Aggregation Behaviour
items.text:
Power BI assigns a default aggregation to every numeric column based on the column's data type and the Summarize by property set in the data model:

Symbol in Fields pane Meaning Σ (sigma) Numeric column — will be aggregated No symbol Text or date column — will be grouped Calculator icon DAX measure — aggregation defined in formula

items.title: Method 1 — Via the Field Well
items.text:
1. In the Visualizations pane, find the field in its well (e.g., Columns, Values, Y-axis).
  2. Click the chevron (∨) or right-click the field name.
  3. Hover over Summarize (or the current aggregation label shown).
  4. Select from the available options.

items.title: Method 2 — Via the Fields Pane
items.text:
Right-click a numeric column directly in the Fields pane:

  1. Right-click the column name.
  2. Select Default summarization.
  3. Choose a summarization method.

This changes the model-level default — the column will use this aggregation everywhere it is added to a new visual.

items.title: Available Aggregation Methods
items.text: Method Description Typical Use Sum Adds all values Revenue, cost, quantity Average Arithmetic mean Order value, rating, temperature Minimum Smallest value Lowest price, earliest date Maximum Largest value Peak sales, highest score Count Number of rows (including nulls) Row count, transaction count Count (Distinct) Number of unique non-null values Unique customers, distinct products Standard deviation Population or sample standard deviation Statistical spread analysis Variance Variance of values Statistical dispersion Median Middle value in sorted list Salary distribution, response time Don't summarize Shows raw values (no aggregation) IDs, codes, keys

items.title: "Don't Summarize" — When to Use It
items.text:
Selecting Don't summarize means Power BI will display the raw value from each row without any calculation. Use this for:

  • Product codes or IDs that happen to be numeric.
  • Rank or order columns that should not be added.
  • Any field where summation is meaningless.

Warning: Adding a non-summarized numeric column to a visual that groups data may produce unexpected results — each group will show one arbitrary value unless the column is unique per group.

items.title: Changing Aggregation for a DAX Measure
items.text:
DAX measures always define their own aggregation in the formula. You cannot change the aggregation of a measure via the field well — the DAX expression is the aggregation.

To use a different aggregation, create a new measure:

Average Sales = AVERAGE(Sales[SalesAmount])
Max Sales     = MAX(Sales[SalesAmount])
Distinct Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])

items.title: Model-Level Default: "Summarize by"
items.text:
The Summarize by property in the data model sets the default aggregation for a column and is visible to every report that uses that model.

To change it:

  1. Go to Data View or Model View.
  2. Select the column.
  3. In the Column tools ribbon, click Summarization and choose the desired default.

Setting this correctly at the model level saves individual report authors from having to change it every time.

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Set the correct Summarize by on all numeric columns at the model level — especially setting ID and code columns to Don't summarize.
  • Use DAX measures for any calculation that requires filters, time intelligence, or conditional logic rather than relying on the visual-level aggregation.
  • Always double-check totals rows — a Count column will show a grand count of rows, not a sum of counts, which can confuse viewers.

items.title: Objective
items.text: Practice changing aggregation methods on a table visual and observe how each method changes the displayed values. By the end you will understand which aggregation is appropriate for different analytical scenarios.

items.title: Setup
items.text: Open the Power BI Desktop file with the training dataset. Add a new report page named "Aggregation Activity".

items.title: Task 1 — Sum (Default)
items.text:
1. Add a Table visual with fields: Category and Sales.
  2. Confirm that Sales is aggregated as Sum (check the chevron in the Values well).
  3. Note the total at the bottom of the table — it is the grand sum of all sales.

Question: Which category has the highest total sales?

items.title: Task 2 — Average
items.text:
1. Click the chevron (∨) next to Sales in the Values well.
  2. Change aggregation to Average.
  3. Observe how the values change.

Question: Which category has the highest average sales per transaction? Is it the same category as the highest total sales?

items.title: Task 3 — Count vs Count (Distinct)
items.text:
1. Add a second table visual on the same page.
  2. Add fields: Region and CustomerID (or an order ID column).
  3. Change the CustomerID aggregation to Count — this counts the number of rows per region.
  4. Duplicate the CustomerID column in the Values well by adding it a second time.
  5. Change the second instance to Count (Distinct) — this counts unique customer IDs.

Question: For any region where Count and Count (Distinct) differ — what does that tell you?

items.title: Task 4 — Minimum and Maximum
items.text:
1. Add a third table visual with: Product and Sales.
  2. Add Sales twice to the Values well.
  3. Set the first to Minimum and rename it "Lowest Sale".
  4. Set the second to Maximum and rename it "Highest Sale".

Question: Which product has the widest range between its minimum and maximum sale values?

items.title: Task 5 — Don't Summarize
items.text:
1. If your dataset has a numeric ID column (e.g., OrderID, ProductID), add it to a table.
  2. Observe that by default it shows a Sum — a meaningless number for an ID.
  3. Change aggregation to Don't summarize.
  4. Note that the column now shows the raw value per row.

items.title: Task 6 — Model-Level Default
items.text:
1. Go to Data View.
  2. Select the OrderID column (or equivalent).
  3. In the Column tools ribbon, change Summarization to Don't summarize.
  4. Return to Report View.
  5. Add the column to a new visual — confirm it no longer defaults to Sum.

items.title: Reflection Questions
items.text:
• When would you use Median instead of Average?
  • Why might Count (Distinct) be more useful than Count for a customer analysis?
  • What is the risk of showing Don't summarize on a category column in a table that groups rows?

items.title: Reference
items.text: • Aggregates in Power BI service – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Overview
items.text: This page provides the answers and explanations for the Methods of Aggregation Practical Activity.

items.title: Task 1 — Sum
items.text:
The Sales column aggregated as Sum shows total revenue per category. The category with the highest bar (or value) in the table is the top revenue contributor across all transactions.

Sum is appropriate here because revenue is additive — $10 from transaction A plus $20 from transaction B legitimately equals $30 total revenue for that category.

items.title: Task 2 — Average
items.text: After switching to Average, the per-category values now represent the typical size of a single transaction within that category.

items.title: Key insight
items.text: The category with the highest average is not necessarily the category with the highest total. A category with a small number of very large transactions can have a higher average than a high-volume, low-value category. Both views tell a different business story — use Sum for revenue analysis, Average for price point or deal-size analysis.

items.title: Task 3 — Count vs Count (Distinct)
items.text:
Column Aggregation Meaning CustomerID (Count) Counts rows Number of orders per region CustomerID (Count Distinct) Counts unique IDs Number of unique customers per region

If Count > Count (Distinct) for a region, it means some customers placed more than one order in that region. The gap between the two numbers tells you the volume of repeat orders.

items.title: When to use each
items.text:
• Count — for measuring activity volume (how many transactions).
  • Count (Distinct) — for measuring audience size (how many unique entities).

items.title: Task 4 — Minimum and Maximum
items.text:
The product with the greatest difference between Minimum and Maximum sale values has the highest price range. This could indicate:

  • A product sold at wildly different quantities per transaction.
  • Discounting applied inconsistently.
  • Different product variants grouped under the same name.
Price Range = [Highest Sale] - [Lowest Sale]

You could create this as a DAX measure to show range directly:

Sales Range = MAX(Sales[SalesAmount]) - MIN(Sales[SalesAmount])

items.title: Task 5 — Don't Summarize
items.text:
Numeric columns used as identifiers (OrderID, ProductID, CustomerID) should never be summed or averaged — those operations are meaningless. Setting Don't summarize makes the column behave like a text identifier in visuals.

If you forget to change this, a table visual will show the sum of all order IDs for a category — a large nonsensical number that will confuse report readers.

items.title: Task 6 — Model-Level Default
items.text: Setting Summarization = Don't summarize at the model level is the best practice. It means every report author who uses this semantic model will get the correct default without needing to remember to change it per visual.

items.title: When would you use Median instead of Average?
items.text: When the distribution is skewed — for example, salary data where a few very high earners would inflate the average. The median represents the "middle" employee better than the average in that case.

items.title: Why might Count (Distinct) be more useful than Count for customer analysis?
items.text: Count tells you how many orders occurred; Count (Distinct) on CustomerID tells you how many different people placed those orders. For a retention analysis, you want to know the number of unique customers, not the total number of orders.

items.title: What is the risk of showing Don't summarize on a category column in a table?
items.text: If the table groups rows by category and the "Don't summarize" column has multiple different values per group, Power BI will display only one arbitrary value (or show an error/blank). Use Don't summarize only on columns that are unique per row in the context of the grouping.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
A table visual displays data in a rows-and-columns grid — the simplest way to present detail-level data, multi-column comparisons, or aggregated summaries. Power BI tables support rich formatting, conditional rules, and interactive cross-filtering.

Reference: Create and Format Table Visualizations in Power BI – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Step 1 — Add a Table Visual
items.text:
1. Open a report page in Report View.
  2. Click an empty area of the canvas (deselect any existing visual).
  3. In the Visualizations pane, click the Table icon (grid with rows and columns).
  4. An empty table placeholder appears on the canvas.

Alternatively, select fields first in the Fields pane — Power BI will auto-choose a visual type, often a table for multi-field selections.

items.title: Step 2 — Add Fields
items.text:
With the table selected, drag columns from the Fields pane into the Columns well (inside the Visualizations pane), or simply click a field checkbox to add it.

Recommended field order:

  1. Dimension columns first (text, categories, dates) — these group rows.
  2. Measure or numeric columns after — these aggregate the values.

Example layout:

Product Category Region Total Sales Units Sold Widget A Hardware North 12,450 312 Widget B Software South 8,900 89

items.title: Step 3 — Resize and Reorder Columns
items.text:
• Resize: Hover over a column border in the table header until the cursor changes, then drag.
  • Reorder: Drag column names within the Columns well in the Visualizations pane.
  • Remove: Click the × next to a field in the Columns well.

items.title: Step 4 — Sort the Table
items.text:
• Click any column header to sort ascending; click again for descending.
  • A small arrow indicator shows the current sort direction.
  • To sort by a field not shown in the table, use the Sort by column feature in the Modeling tab.

items.title: Step 5 — Resize the Visual on Canvas
items.text:
• Drag the handles at the corners and edges of the visual frame.
  • Hold Shift while resizing to maintain aspect ratio.
  • Use View › Align and View › Distribute to precisely position multiple visuals.

items.title: Totals Row
items.text:
Power BI automatically adds a Total row at the bottom of tables for numeric columns.

  • Show totals: Format pane › Totals › toggle on/off.
  • Totals use the same aggregation as the column (e.g., Sum of Sales, Count of Orders).
  • For measures, the total reflects the measure evaluated over the entire visible data.

Note: The total row for a measure is not necessarily the sum of visible row values — it evaluates the DAX expression at the full filter context.

items.title: Column Aggregation Behaviour
items.text:
When you add a numeric column (not a measure) to a table, Power BI defaults to Sum. You can change this per-column:

  1. Right-click the field in the Columns well.
  2. Hover over Summarize (or the aggregation name shown).
  3. Choose: Sum, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Count, Count (Distinct), Standard Deviation, Variance, Median, or Don't summarize.

Reference: Change How a Visual Aggregates Data – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Keep tables to 5–8 columns maximum for readability.
  • Place tables on a detail page accessed via drill-through, rather than cluttering summary dashboards.
  • Use measures instead of raw numeric columns for calculated aggregations — this gives you full DAX control.
  • Enable Autofit column width (Format pane) so column widths adjust to content automatically.

items.title: References
items.text:
• Create and Format Table Visualizations – Microsoft Learn
  • Overview of visualizations in Power BI – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Cross-filtering is the mechanism by which selecting a data point in one visual automatically filters or highlights the other visuals on the same report page. It is one of the most powerful interactivity features in Power BI and requires no code — it works by default between most visual types.

Reference: How visuals cross-filter each other in a Power BI report – Microsoft Learn

items.title: How Cross-Filtering Works
items.text:
When a user clicks a row in a table (or a bar in a chart, a slice of a pie, etc.), Power BI injects a temporary filter into the report's filter context. Every other visual on the page re-evaluates its data against that filter.

Two modes exist:

Mode Visual Behaviour Cross-filter Other visuals show only the matching rows (non-matching rows hidden) Cross-highlight Other visuals dim non-matching data but keep the visual structure visible

By default, clicking a table row cross-highlights bar and column charts, while it cross-filters other table and matrix visuals.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Place a Table visual on the canvas with columns: Category, Region, Sales.
  2. Place a Clustered column chart on the same page: Category on X-axis, Sales on Y-axis.

items.title: Interaction
items.text:
• Click the row for Category = Hardware in the table.
  • The column chart highlights the Hardware bar; other bars are dimmed.
  • The table itself highlights only the Hardware rows.
  • Click away (or press Esc) to clear the selection.

items.title: Editing Visual Interactions
items.text:
You can control how each pair of visuals interacts:

  1. Select the visual that will drive the filter (the source).
  2. Go to Format ribbon tab.
  3. Click Edit interactions — icons appear on all other visuals.
Icon Effect Funnel (filter) Applies cross-filter (hides non-matching data) Bar chart (highlight) Applies cross-highlight (dims non-matching data) Circle with line (none) No interaction from this source
  1. Click the desired icon on each target visual.
  2. Click Edit interactions again to exit interaction-edit mode.

Reference: Change How Visuals Interact in a Report – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Slicers vs Cross-Filter
items.text: Slicers always cross-filter (they filter, not highlight). A slicer selection removes non-matching data from all visuals it affects. A table row click, by contrast, uses cross-highlight by default for chart visuals. You can change this with Edit interactions.

items.title: Multi-Select Cross-Filter
items.text: Hold Ctrl and click multiple rows in a table to filter/highlight by multiple values simultaneously. For example, clicking Hardware then Ctrl + click Software will show data for both categories in other visuals.

items.title: Drill-Through vs Cross-Filter
items.text:
Feature Scope Mechanism Cross-filter Same page Click a data point Drill-through Navigates to another page Right-click › Drill through

Cross-filtering is ephemeral (clears on click-away); drill-through navigates to a dedicated detail page and persists filters until you navigate back.

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Use Edit interactions › None to prevent a logo or decorative visual from triggering filters accidentally.
  • Disable cross-highlighting on KPI cards if you want them to always show the grand total — set interaction to None from every other visual.
  • Test cross-filter behavior during development by clicking every visual on the page to ensure interactions behave as expected.
  • Document intended interaction patterns in a tooltip or info button on the report page.

items.title: References
items.text:
• How visuals cross-filter each other – Microsoft Learn
  • Change How Visuals Interact in a Report – Microsoft Learn
  • Filters and highlighting in Power BI reports – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Power BI offers extensive formatting options for table visuals — from quick preset styles to per-column conditional rules based on data values. Good formatting makes data scannable and draws attention to what matters.

Reference: Create and Format Table Visualizations – Microsoft Learn Reference: Apply Conditional Table Formatting – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Accessing Format Options
items.text:
1. Select the table visual.
  2. In the Visualizations pane, click the Format visual tab (paint roller icon).
  3. Expand sections: Style presets, Grid, Column headers, Values, Totals, Specific columns.

items.title: Style Presets
items.text:
The quickest way to apply a consistent look:

Preset Description None Minimal, borderless grid Minimal Thin lines, light headers Bold header Dark header row, white text Alternating rows Banded rows for readability Contrast alternating rows High-contrast banding Flashy rows Stronger color accent Condensed Reduced row height

Select a preset under Format visual › Style presets to apply it instantly, then override individual settings below it.

items.title: Grid Settings
items.text: Option Effect Horizontal gridlines Show/hide lines between rows Vertical gridlines Show/hide lines between columns Row padding Set padding (pixels) above/below cell text Text size Global font size for the table body Font family Choose a font for all cells

items.title: Column Headers
items.text: Option Effect Font color Header text color Background color Header background color Font size Header text size Bold / Italic / Underline Text decoration Alignment Left, center, or right Text wrap Allow long headers to wrap Auto size column width Fit column width to content

items.title: Values (Body Cells)
items.text:
Same controls as column headers, applied to data rows:

  • Background color, font color, font size, font family, bold/italic.
  • Alternating row colors — set two colors for banded rows.

items.title: Conditional Formatting
items.text:
Conditional formatting applies dynamic visual cues based on data values. To add it:

  1. Right-click (or click the chevron ∨) on a column in the Columns well.
  2. Select Conditional formatting.
  3. Choose a format type:
Type What It Shows Background color Fill cell background by value or rule Font color Color text by value or rule Data bars Horizontal in-cell bar proportional to value Icons KPI-style symbols (arrows, shapes, flags) Web URL Make cell text a clickable hyperlink

items.title: Background Color — Gradient
items.text:
Applies a continuous color scale between a minimum and maximum value.

  1. Select Background color.
  2. Set Format style to Gradient.
  3. Define Minimum and Maximum colors and their corresponding values.

Result: cells shade from one color to another proportionally.

items.title: Background Color — Rules
items.text:
Applies discrete color based on threshold rules.

  1. Set Format style to Rules.
  2. Add rules: if value is between X and Y, color is green.
  3. Stack multiple rules — they are evaluated top-to-bottom.

items.title: Data Bars
items.text:
Renders a fill bar inside each cell proportional to its value relative to the column range.

  • Set Minimum and Maximum bar values.
  • Choose Positive and Negative bar colors.
  • Enable Show bar only to hide the text value.

items.title: Icons
items.text:
Displays icons (up/down arrows, circles, flags, etc.) alongside or instead of the value.

  1. Define the number of icon sets (3, 4, or 5 icons).
  2. Set threshold rules for each icon.
  3. Choose Icon layout: Left of data, Right of data, or Data only.

Reference: Conditional formatting in Power BI visuals – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Specific Column Overrides
items.text:
Under Format visual › Specific columns, you can override formatting for a single column independently of the rest:

  • Select the column name from the dropdown.
  • Change font, background, alignment, display units, and decimal places for that column only.

items.title: Totals Row Formatting
items.text:
Under Format visual › Totals:

  • Toggle the totals row on or off.
  • Set a separate background color and font color for the total row.
  • Adjust font size and bold independently of body cells.

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Use alternating row colors for tables with many rows — it reduces the chance of reading the wrong row.
  • Apply background color conditional formatting to KPI columns so under-performers stand out immediately.
  • Keep conditional formatting consistent across related tables in the same report.
  • Reserve data bars for a single key metric column — too many bars create visual noise.
  • Use specific column overrides to right-align numeric columns and left-align text columns.

items.title: References
items.text:
• Create and Format Table Visualizations – Microsoft Learn
  • Apply Conditional Table Formatting – Microsoft Learn
  • Conditional formatting in Power BI visuals – Microsoft Learn
  • Expression-based titles in Power BI Desktop – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Overview
items.text:
This section covers two of the most important structured visuals in Power BI: the Matrix and Cards. The Matrix is the tabular pivot visual that replaces traditional cross-tab spreadsheet views. Cards display single KPI values prominently and clearly.

Together these two visuals form the backbone of most executive dashboards and summary pages.

items.title: Section Contents
items.text: Topic Description Matrix Visualization Row/column/value wells, drill-down, subtotals, conditional formatting Cards Visualization Card types, KPI visual, multi-row card, new card visual Practical Activity Hands-on activity building matrix and card visuals Activity — Completed Reference solutions with explanations

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Familiarity with the Visualizations pane (Build / Format / Analytics tabs).
  • A loaded dataset with at least one numeric measure and one or more dimension columns.
  • Basic understanding of cross-filtering from the Tables section.

items.title: References
items.text:
• Matrix visual in Power BI – Microsoft Learn
  • Card visual in Power BI – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Objective
items.text: Build a summary page using card visuals and a matrix visual that work together interactively. You will practice assigning fields to matrix wells, enabling drill-down, formatting cards with conditional color, and verifying cross-filter behavior between the matrix and cards.

items.title: Setup
items.text: Open the training Power BI Desktop file and add a new report page named "Cards & Matrix Activity".

items.title: Task A1 — Total Sales Card
items.text:
1. Add a Card visual to the top-left of the canvas.
  2. Drag the Sales measure (or column set to Sum) into the Callout value well.
  3. In Format visual › Callout value, set:
  4. Display units: Millions (M)
  5. Decimal places: 1
  6. Rename the card title to "Total Revenue" via Format visual › General › Title.

items.title: Task A2 — Total Units Card
items.text:
1. Add a second Card visual next to the first.
  2. Add the Units field (Sum) as the callout value.
  3. Set display units to Thousands (K), 1 decimal place.
  4. Title: "Units Sold"

items.title: Task A3 — Average Order Value Card
items.text:
1. Create a DAX measure in your model:
Avg Order Value = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), COUNT(Sales[OrderID]))
  1. Add a third Card visual with this measure.
  2. Format: no display units, 2 decimal places, title "Avg Order Value".

items.title: Task A4 — Conditional Card Color
items.text:
1. Select the Total Revenue card.
  2. Go to Format visual › Callout value → Font color → Conditional formatting (fx).
  3. Set a rule: if value is greater than your target (e.g., 1,000,000), color is green; else red.

items.title: Task B1 — Build the Matrix
items.text:
1. Add a Matrix visual to the lower half of the canvas.
  2. Assign fields:
  3. Rows: Category → Product
  4. Columns: Year → Quarter (use the Date hierarchy if available)
  5. Values: Sales (Sum)

items.title: Task B2 — Enable Subtotals
items.text:
1. In Format visual:
  2. Enable Row subtotals — shows a subtotal row per Category.
  3. Enable Column subtotals — shows a subtotal column per Year.
  4. Enable Grand total for rows and columns.

items.title: Task B3 — Conditional Formatting on the Matrix
items.text:
1. Click the chevron next to Sum of Sales in the Values well.
  2. Select Conditional formatting › Background color.
  3. Apply a gradient from white (lowest) to amber/orange (highest).

items.title: Task B4 — Drill Down
items.text:
1. Click the ↓ button in the matrix header to expand all categories to their products.
  2. Click the ↑ button to collapse back.
  3. Right-click a single category row and select Drill down to expand only that category.

items.title: Task C1 — Cross-Filter Cards from Matrix
items.text:
1. Click a Category row in the matrix.
  2. Observe that all three card visuals update to show totals for that category only.
  3. Press Esc or click away to clear the filter.

items.title: Task C2 — Verify Card Totals
items.text:
1. Confirm that the cards show grand totals when nothing is selected.
  2. Select one year in the column headers — confirm cards update to that year's data.

items.title: Checklist
items.text: Task Done Three card visuals created and formatted ☐ Avg Order Value DAX measure created ☐ Conditional color on Total Revenue card ☐ Matrix with Category/Product rows and Year/Quarter columns ☐ Subtotals and grand totals enabled ☐ Conditional formatting on matrix values ☐ Drill-down tested ☐ Cross-filter from matrix to cards tested ☐

items.title: References
items.text:
• Create a Matrix Visual in Power BI – Microsoft Learn
  • Create a card visual in Power BI – Microsoft Learn
  • CALCULATE function (DAX) – Microsoft Learn

items.title: Overview
items.text: This page provides the solutions and explanations for the Cards and Matrix Practical Activity.

items.title: Task A1 — Total Sales Card
items.text:
The card should display a single large number formatted as millions (e.g., $4.2M). Setting display units to Millions and decimal places to 1 keeps the number readable without overwhelming the viewer with digits.

The title field is found under Format visual › General › Title › Title text. Always title cards clearly — a number without context is meaningless on a dashboard.

items.title: Task A2 — Total Units Card
items.text: Similar setup with Thousands as the display unit. $3.1K units is more scannable than 3,145.

items.title: Task A3 — Avg Order Value Measure
items.text:
The correct DAX expression:

Avg Order Value = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), COUNT(Sales[OrderID]))

Using DIVIDE instead of / prevents a divide-by-zero error if there are no orders in the current filter context. The result should show no display units and 2 decimal places — for example, $47.32.

items.title: Why not use AVERAGE directly?
items.text: AVERAGE(Sales[SalesAmount]) computes the average of the SalesAmount column — which is the average value per row. If each row already represents one order, this is equivalent. But if a row can contain multiple items, you need to compute total revenue divided by a distinct count of orders. Always understand your data grain before choosing the formula.

items.title: Task A4 — Conditional Card Color
items.text:
The conditional formatting dialog (accessed via the fx button next to Font color) lets you define rules. Example rule:

Rule Color Value ≥ 1,000,000 Green (#107C10) Value < 1,000,000 Red (#D83B01)

This gives instant visual feedback on whether the target has been met.

items.title: Task B1 — Matrix Field Assignment
items.text:
Well Fields Result Rows Category → Product Two-level hierarchy; drill-down available Columns Year → Quarter Time axis across the top Values Sales (Sum) Revenue at each intersection

A correctly built matrix shows revenue by product broken down by quarter — a classic cross-tab for performance analysis.

items.title: Task B2 — Subtotals
items.text: Enabling row subtotals adds a Category Total row after each category's products. Column subtotals add an Annual Total column after each year's quarters. The grand total cell (bottom-right) shows the overall revenue across all filters.

items.title: Task B3 — Conditional Formatting
items.text: The amber gradient draws the eye to the cells with the highest revenue. Because the gradient scales to the visible min/max, filtering by a slicer or cross-filter recalibrates the color scale automatically.

items.title: Task B4 — Drill-Down
items.text:
• The ↓ button expands all category rows to product level simultaneously.
  • Right-clicking a single category and choosing Drill down expands only that category — useful when you have many categories and want to focus on one.
  • The Expand all down one level in the hierarchy button (⊞) is different from Drill down — it shows both the category row and its product rows at the same time.

items.title: Cross-Filter Behavior
items.text:
When you click a matrix row, all card visuals on the page re-evaluate their DAX measures with that row's filter context applied. This is how a single page becomes interactive without any additional configuration.

If a card does not update when you click the matrix, check Format → Edit interactions and ensure the card is set to Filter (not None) from the matrix.
